**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Paper 2: Section A - Summary and Text Reconstruction; Section B - Composition; Section C - Prescribed Texts. Duration: three hours.**

Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will be penalised.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised composition will be severely sanctioned.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **a)** Write a story which illustrates the idiomatic expression, "Curiosity killed the cat."
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Open with the idiom and announce the narrator's own experience (Limbe, Mbella).
2. Present the warning: the locked shed, Uncle Etongo's rule.
3. Build the temptation and the act: the key, the open drum.
4. Show the consequences: hospital, uncle arrested, family shame.
5. End with the lesson: ignore the warning signs at your own risk.

**Model composition (540 words)**

Every child in our neighbourhood in Limbe has heard the old proverb that curiosity killed the cat, but few believe it until it touches their own lives. I certainly did not, until the afternoon when my own curiosity nearly cost me my life.

My name is Mbella, and at sixteen I was known throughout the quarter as the boy who asked too many questions. I wanted to know why the sea was salty and what my uncle kept in the locked shed behind his boat house. Uncle Etongo was a gentle fisherman, yet on one subject he was as hard as iron. "Never go near that shed," he told me on the first day of the holidays. "What is in there is not for children." I nodded politely, but the warning only made the shed more attractive to me than a sweet shop.

For two weeks I watched that little building. Each evening Uncle returned from the sea and locked the door with a heavy padlock. The key hung round his neck like a charm. My imagination ran wild: perhaps there was treasure, perhaps a secret. Then, on a Sunday when the whole family had gone to church, I found the key lying on the kitchen table, where he had left it after changing his shirt. My heart pounded. A sensible boy would have put it back, but I was not sensible; I was curious.

I tiptoed across the yard, turned the key and pushed the door open. A sharp, bitter smell struck my nose at once. In the dim light I saw rows of plastic drums, and one of them had its lid half open. I bent over it to look inside. A cloud of strong fumes rose into my face. My eyes burned, my throat closed, and the shed began to spin around me. I tried to shout, but I collapsed on the dusty floor.

When I woke up, I was lying in the Limbe Regional Hospital with a drip in my arm, and my mother was weeping beside the bed. The doctor explained that the drums contained a chemical which dishonest fishermen use to poison fish in the river. Using it was illegal and deadly, and my uncle, tempted by easy profit, had hidden it from everyone. A neighbour had found me; a quarter of an hour later, and I would not have lived to tell this tale.

The consequences did not end in the hospital. The police, alerted by the doctor, arrested my uncle, and the fishermen's union banned him from the harbour. For weeks I lay on my bed in pain, unable to eat, ashamed that my inquisitiveness had destroyed a man who had always loved me. Uncle Etongo never blamed me, but the sadness in his eyes was heavier than any punishment.

Today I still ask questions, because curiosity is the engine of learning, but I now ask them with care. I have learnt that some doors are closed for good reasons, that a warning from an elder is often a shield, and that seeking knowledge is not the same as prying. The cat in the proverb did not die because it was clever; it died because it ignored the signs that said "stop".

**Marking grid (20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Telling any story: the plot must make the idiom true (a curious act with harmful consequences), and the ending must show it.
2. Rushing the consequences or ending without a lesson, so the idiom is never illustrated.
